discovery: Discovery of high-energy cosmic neutrinos and the founding of neutrino astronomy with the IceCube Neutrino Observatory
motivation: The nominees conceived, designed and realized the first cubic-kilometre neutrino telescope, transforming the deep Antarctic ice into a particle detector. Building on the pioneering AMANDA and Baikal efforts, IceCube discovered in 2013 a diffuse flux of astrophysical neutrinos at TeV-PeV energies, opening a genuinely new window onto the universe. It went on to identify the first neutrino sources: the blazar TXS 0506+056, through a real-time alert and multi-messenger follow-up (2018), and the Seyfert galaxy NGC 1068 (2022), and mapped neutrino emission from the Galactic plane (2023). These results show that hadronic cosmic accelerators exist and that neutrinos can be used to locate them, probing regions that photons cannot reach. Halzen led the vision and the collaboration, Karle led detector construction and the discovery analyses, and Spiering pioneered large-volume neutrino telescopes in water and ice. Their work created a field.
